patterns.name: Typed handoff tool with declared destination, argument schema, and history input_filter
patterns.what: A handoff is not an internal function call - it is rendered to the model as a tool named transfer_to_<agent_name> (Handoff.default_tool_name()). handoff(agent, tool_name_override=, on_handoff=, input_type=, input_filter=, is_enabled=) declares it. input_type is the Pydantic schema for the handoff tool-call arguments: the SDK publishes it as the tool's `parameters`, validates the returned JSON locally, and passes the parsed value to on_handoff(ctx, input_data). is_enabled is evaluated while preparing available handoffs, before the model returns arguments, so it cannot authorize values inside an argument-bearing handoff; field-level authorization must happen at the top of on_handoff and must raise to refuse (the transfer continues once on_handoff returns normally). input_filter receives HandoffInputData and must return a new HandoffInputData - that is the only supported way to change what history the receiving agent sees. handoff_filters.remove_all_tools strips structured tool items but does not redact tool text already copied into ordinary messages. RunConfig.handoff_input_filter is a run-wide default and a per-handoff input_filter wins over it. Optional history compaction: RunConfig.nest_handoff_history wraps summarizable history into ordered <CONVERSATION HISTORY> segments while preserving lossless message items in place, with RunConfig.handoff_history_mapper as a full override; nesting applies only when neither the handoff's input_filter nor the run's handoff_input_filter is set.
patterns.why: hermes-day currently routes with regex plus a judgment lane, which means a routing decision is not a typed object. Handoffs make the destination, the payload schema, and the receiver's visible history all declared and independently assertable - and the is_enabled/on_handoff split is a real correctness lesson (visibility filters are not authorization).
patterns.build: Add hday_router.Handoff(destination_lane, tool_name='transfer_to_<lane>', input_model: type[BaseModel]|None, on_handoff: Callable[[RunContext, BaseModel], Awaitable[None]]|None, input_filter: Callable[[HandoffInputData], HandoffInputData]|None, is_enabled: Callable[[], bool]|None). HandoffInputData = frozen dataclass(input_history: list[Msg], pre_handoff_items: list[Msg], new_items: list[Msg], input_items: list[Msg]|None). Render enabled handoffs into the model's tool list with input_model.model_json_schema() as `parameters`. On a transfer_to_* call: validate args -> if invalid, return a tool error and do not transfer -> run on_handoff -> apply input_filter -> build the receiver's messages -> append one handoff record to the unified decision ledger {from_lane, to_lane, tool_name, args_hash, ts, enabled_reason}. Provide hday_router.filters.remove_all_tools as the default filter and RunConfig-equivalent handoff_input_filter on the lane config with per-handoff precedence.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert the rendered tool list contains exactly one transfer_to_gate entry whose parameters equal the input_model schema; (b) feed a malformed arg dict and assert on_handoff was never called and no ledger record was written; (c) with input_filter=remove_all_tools assert tool_call/tool_output items are dropped and plain messages preserved; (d) assert per-handoff input_filter beats the lane-level handoff_input_filter; (e) assert is_enabled=False removes the tool from the list entirely.

patterns.name: Guardrails as typed verdicts with tripwires, plus a parallel-vs-blocking execution switch
patterns.what: Guardrails are decorated functions (@input_guardrail, @output_guardrail) that return GuardrailFunctionOutput(output_info=<any>, tripwire_triggered=<bool>), wrapped by the runner into InputGuardrailResult / OutputGuardrailResult. If tripwire_triggered is true the runner raises InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered / OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered and halts. Two execution strategies: run_in_parallel=True (default) starts the guardrail concurrently with the agent - lowest latency, but the agent may already have consumed tokens and executed tools before cancellation; run_in_parallel=False runs the guardrail to completion BEFORE the agent starts, so a tripwire prevents token spend and tool side effects (output guardrails always run after the agent, so they have no run_in_parallel). Input guardrails run only for the FIRST agent in a chain. The exception carries evidence: exception.guardrail_result identifies the triggering guardrail, and exception.run_data.input_guardrail_results / output_guardrail_results hold every result completed before the stop, including the tripwire. Tool-level guardrails (tool_input_guardrails / tool_output_guardrails) exist on the FunctionTool pipeline and can be attached to every tool of a local MCP server; hosted tools and built-in execution tools do not use that pipeline. A tripwire and an exception raised by the guardrail function behave differently on persistence: a tripwire persists already-completed tool call/output items and reasoning needed for replay while EXCLUDING the rejected candidate final output, substituting the text 'Output withheld by an output guardrail.'; a raised exception is treated as an unknown verdict and persists completed final-turn items. RunConfig.output_guardrail_blocked_message can replace the placeholder with a data-free string or synchronous formatter that never receives the rejected output.
patterns.why: The hday gate already produces a verdict, but the verdict is not a typed object with a run-scoped evidence bundle, and it has no declared latency/cost tradeoff. The tripwire-vs-exception persistence rule is directly reusable: our ledger must record the gated attempt without storing the rejected payload.
patterns.build: Introduce hday_gate.GuardrailResult(guardrail_name, output_info, tripwire_triggered) and a @guardrail(kind='input'|'output', run_in_parallel: bool) decorator registering into a lane's guardrail lists. Gate returns a GuardrailResult instead of raising, and the runner converts tripwire=True into GateTripwire(lane, guardrail_name, run_data). Implement the persistence rule in the ledger writer: on tripwire, append tool_call/tool_output records plus the guardrail result with output_info replaced by a constant placeholder, and never append the candidate output; on a guardrail exception, append the completed final-turn items and mark verdict='unknown'. Add RunConfig.tripwire_placeholder so the placeholder text is configurable but never derived from rejected content. Keep input guardrails first-agent-only, matching the reference semantics.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) a stub guardrail returning tripwire_triggered=True raises GateTripwire and the ledger contains zero records carrying the rejected payload (assert by substring scan of the serialized ledger); (b) with run_in_parallel=False assert the tool executor was never invoked (spy counter == 0) when the guardrail trips, and was invoked when run_in_parallel=True; (c) assert input guardrails registered on a second lane in a chain never execute; (d) assert GateTripwire.run_data.input_guardrail_results includes the triggering result.

patterns.name: Session as a five-method pluggable store with a merge callback and a per-run fetch limit
patterns.what: A session is a narrow interface, not a framework feature: get_items(limit=...) -> list, add_items(items), pop_item(), clear_session(), and the session_id key. Runner.run(..., session=session) merges session history with the current call's input before the model call; RunConfig.session_input_callback receives the two lists and returns the merged list, which is the sanctioned seam for 'keep recent history only' style policies. RunConfig.session_settings=SessionSettings(limit=None|N) controls how much history is fetched before each run (None = all, N = most recent N). Implementations ship as a matrix over the same interface - SQLiteSession (file-backed or in-memory), AsyncSQLiteSession (aiosqlite), AdvancedSQLiteSession (branching/analytics) - and SQLiteSession(session_id, db_path) takes an optional database file. pop_item() is documented for corrections: pop the assistant item then the user item to undo a turn. Session stores items as a list of message-shaped dicts, and the runner is responsible for writing back what happened.
patterns.why: hermes-day's ledger is append-only and global; a session object with an explicit merge callback gives us per-conversation history with a testable truncation policy, and pop_item gives the cockpit an undo primitive without mutating the ledger.
patterns.build: Define hday_sessions.SessionStore protocol {get_items(session_id, limit=None), add_items(session_id, items), pop_item(session_id), clear_session(session_id)} with a SqliteSessionStore implementation on the existing sqlite handle plus an in-memory store for tests. Add HdayRunConfig.session_input_callback(existing: list, new: list) -> list invoked before every lane call, and session_settings=SessionSettings(limit=...). Wire the cockpit's 'undo last turn' button to pop_item twice (assistant then user) and record the undo as a decision-ledger entry so the ledger stays the audit source of truth while the session stays the working set.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) with SessionSettings(limit=3) and 10 stored items assert the callback receives exactly 3; (b) assert a custom session_input_callback's return value is what reaches the model (capture via a fake provider); (c) assert pop_item twice then get_items yields the original prefix; (d) assert clear_session leaves the decision ledger untouched.

patterns.name: Trace as a typed span tree with custom span types and additive processors
patterns.what: One trace is a tree of typed spans. A Trace has trace_id (format trace_<32 alphanumeric>) and a name; each Span has trace_id, span_id, parent_id, started_at/finished_at, and span_data, a typed payload (AgentSpanData, GenerationSpanData, FunctionSpanData, GuardrailSpanData, HandoffSpanData, ...). The runner auto-instruments: Runner.{run,run_sync,run_streamed} is wrapped in trace(), each agent run in agent_span(), each LLM generation in generation_span(), each function tool call in function_span(), each guardrail in guardrail_span(), each handoff in handoff_span(); custom_span() exists for anything else. trace() is usable as a context manager (`with trace('Joke workflow') as t:`) and wrapping multiple run() calls in one trace() groups them into a single trace - which is the documented way to express 'these runs are one unit of work'. Export is processor-based: BatchTraceProcessor batches to a BackendSpanExporter with a size trigger and a final flush at process exit; add_trace_processor() ADDS an observer alongside the default, set_trace_processors() REPLACES the set. Processors are independent observers and the default provider catches a processor's callback exceptions so one failing processor does not stop the others - therefore a redaction processor registered before an exporter does NOT protect that exporter; when export depends on redaction, redaction and delivery must live inside one application-owned exporter. flush_traces() blocks until buffered spans are exported and should be called after trace() closes. RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data=False disables capturing generation/function inputs and outputs.
patterns.why: We have a decision ledger but no span tree, so there is no way to answer 'what did lane X do inside turn Y'. The span_data typing plus the processor-is-not-a-filter lesson map straight onto our honesty guard and ledger writer.
patterns.build: Add hday_trace.py: dataclasses Trace(trace_id, name, started_at, finished_at, spans) and Span(trace_id, span_id, parent_id, started_at, finished_at, span_type, span_data: dict). Span constructors mirror the reference set: agent_span, generation_span, function_span, guardrail_span, handoff_span, custom_span, all context managers that set parent_id from a contextvar. Wrap every lane dispatch in trace() and every gate decision in guardrail_span() carrying the GuardrailResult. Export via TraceProcessor protocol with add_trace_processor (additive, default ledger writer stays registered) and set_trace_processors (replace). Enforce the reference's safety rule: the ledger exporter must redact before it writes and must never rely on a separate redaction processor - if redaction raises, discard the batch and log a fixed message with no payload. Add RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data and flush_traces().
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) run a two-lane turn and assert the resulting trace has one root agent_span per lane with correct parent_id chaining and exactly one guardrail_span per gate call; (b) assert wrapping two lane runs in one trace() yields a single Trace with two root agent spans; (c) assert add_trace_processor leaves the ledger writer registered while set_trace_processors removes it; (d) inject a redaction failure and assert nothing was written and the log line contains no payload substring; (e) assert trace_include_sensitive_data=False nulls generation span inputs/outputs.

patterns.name: Declared tool surface: hosted tools, deferred loading via namespaces + ToolSearchTool, and agents-as-tools with approval
patterns.what: Four distinct tool classes share one declaration site on Agent(tools=[...]). (1) Hosted tools run on the provider side: WebSearchTool, FileSearchTool, CodeInterpreterTool, HostedMCPTool, ImageGenerationTool. (2) Local/runtime tools require an implementation you supply: ComputerTool (Computer/AsyncComputer interface), ApplyPatchTool (ApplyPatchEditor interface), ShellTool (local OR hosted container - with a hosted environment you must not set executor, needs_approval, or on_approval). (3) Deferred loading: @function_tool(defer_loading=True), tool_namespace(name=, description=, tools=[...]), and HostedMCPTool(tool_config={..., 'defer_loading': True}) are searchable surfaces; the agent then needs exactly one ToolSearchTool() to let the model load them on demand. Namespaces can mix immediate and deferred tools - non-deferred members stay callable immediately. ToolSearchTool(execution='client') is rejected by the standard Runner (client-executed tool_search_call raises). (4) allowed_callers controls how a tool may be invoked: omitted = direct model calls only, ['programmatic'] = program-only, ['direct','programmatic'] = both; ProgrammaticToolCallingTool() must appear at most once and requires at least one programmatically callable tool or a searchable surface. For @function_tool(allowed_callers=[...]) a structured return annotation (Pydantic/TypedDict/dataclass) becomes a strict output schema validated before the value returns to the program. Separately, Agent.as_tool() turns a whole agent into a tool and accepts max_turns, run_config, hooks, session, needs_approval, plus structured input via parameters / input_builder / include_input_schema, output shaping via custom_output_extractor, streaming observation via on_stream, and runtime gating via is_enabled. The docs are explicit that is_enabled controls visibility and dispatch and does NOT replace authorization on arguments or the accessed resource.
patterns.why: hermes-day has tools but no notion of a deferred or gated tool surface, and our subagent dispatch is not a declared tool. Copying the four-class split plus ToolSearchTool gives us a small tool budget with on-demand expansion, and as_tool(needs_approval=, is_enabled=, custom_output_extractor=) gives the router a uniform way to expose sub-lanes.
patterns.build: In hday_tools.py split tool registration into classes: HostedTool (no local executor, provider-side), LocalTool(executor, needs_approval, on_approval), DeferredTool(namespace), and AgentTool (sub-lane). Implement tool_namespace(name, description, tools) grouping deferred tools, plus ToolSearchTool() which searches namespace names/descriptions and loads matching tools into the active set. Implement allowed_callers on the tool record and reject a tool_search_call emitted with execution='client' in the runner (raise, do not execute). Implement lane.as_tool(tool_name, description, parameters, input_builder, include_input_schema, custom_output_extractor, on_stream, needs_approval, is_enabled) where needs_approval routes into the existing gate escalation path and is_enabled is a static-config predicate only - document in the gate module that argument-level authorization belongs in the tool body or the guardrail, never in is_enabled.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a namespace with 3 deferred and 1 immediate tool exposes exactly 1 tool before ToolSearchTool runs and 4 after; (b) assert exactly one ToolSearchTool is accepted and a second is rejected; (c) assert a client-executed tool_search_call raises instead of executing; (d) assert allowed_callers=['programmatic'] makes the tool invisible to direct calls but reachable from the program runner; (e) assert as_tool(needs_approval=True) produces an interruption record and resumes only after approve(); (f) assert is_enabled=False removes the agent tool from the model's tool list.

patterns.name: Subagent definition file with a frontmatter contract that constrains tools, model, permissions, skills and hooks
patterns.what: A subagent is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter plus a system-prompt body, and the frontmatter is the whole contract: name (required), description (required - the parent uses it to decide when to delegate), tools (an allowlist; omitting it inherits every tool), disallowedTools, model (model | inherit), permission-mode, skills, hooks, and memory. Files are discovered from user, project, and plugin scopes with a documented precedence, and a subagent can be created through the /agents command, the CLI, or by hand. Two invocation paths: automatic (the parent delegates based on the description) and explicit (the user names the subagent). Key operational facts: subagents run with their OWN context window and cannot see the parent's conversation except through what the parent passes in the delegation prompt; they cannot spawn further subagents (no nesting); and there is a documented concurrency limit for parallel subagent execution. Context management is first-class: a subagent can be given a persistent identity (worktree-isolated and/or background) so it survives across turns, and its transcript can be retrieved afterwards, with per-subagent transcript files. There is also a fork mode (CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT) where a subagent inherits the parent's full conversation instead of starting clean.
patterns.why: Our lanes are code, not declarative artifacts, so tuning a lane's tool access means editing the harness. A frontmatter contract gives us versioned, per-lane capability declarations that the manifest lane can lint - and 'subagents cannot nest' plus 'each has its own context window' are exactly the constraints we need to state explicitly in hday_manifest.
patterns.build: Add hday_manifest.SubagentSpec parsed from .hday/agents/<name>.md YAML frontmatter: name, description, tools (list|None=inherit), disallowedTools, model ('inherit' or explicit), permission_mode, skills, hooks, memory. Lane loader resolves specs across scopes (user < project < plugin) with documented precedence and validates: name unique, description non-empty, tools subset of the registered tool registry, no nesting (a subagent spec must not declare `agents`). Delegation passes an explicit prompt payload because the child context is fresh; a `fork: true` flag makes the child inherit the parent's message list instead. Add a max_concurrent_subagents setting enforced by a semaphore in the dispatcher, and write each child's transcript to runs/agents/<lane>/<run_id>.jsonl retrievable by the cockpit.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a spec with tools=['read','grep'] cannot invoke a write tool even when the parent can; (b) assert omitting tools inherits the full registry; (c) assert a spec declaring nested agents fails manifest validation with a specific error; (d) assert two subagent specs with the same name resolve by scope precedence and the loser is reported; (e) assert max_concurrent_subagents=2 serializes three delegations (assert peak observed concurrency == 2); (f) assert fork=True puts the parent's messages in the child's first request and fork=False does not.

patterns.name: Lifecycle hook system: many events, matcher groups, five handler types, exit-code and JSON verdict semantics
patterns.what: Hooks fire at named lifecycle points and are configured as event -> matcher groups -> handlers. The event surface is broad and includes PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, Stop, StopFailure, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, Notification, ConfigChange, InstructionsLoaded, CwdChanged, FileChanged, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch, Elicitation, ElicitationResult, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, TeammateIdle and MessageDisplay. A handler is one of five types - shell command, HTTP endpoint, MCP tool call, LLM prompt, or subagent - so the extension point is not tied to the shell. The matcher field filters activation: a plain value or |-separated alternatives is compared against the event's matcher field (tool_name for tool events); a matcher containing other characters is treated as a JavaScript regular expression tested with RegExp.prototype.test, which matches anywhere in the value, so ^Edit$ is needed for whole-string matching; some events have no matcher support and a matcher on them is silently ignored; MCP tools match as mcp__<server>__<tool> and a server-wide match requires the .* suffix (mcp__memory alone is an exact string that matches nothing). Input arrives as JSON on stdin (command hooks) or as the POST body (HTTP hooks); output can be plain text or JSON with fields including permissionDecision, and additionalContext can inject text back into the model's context. Exit codes carry semantics, and there is an `if` field for a second, narrower filter beyond the matcher, plus async hooks and a `once`-style single-fire option. Config lives in user settings, project settings, or a plugin's hooks/hooks.json, and the same events fire in terminal, IDE, desktop and cloud sessions.
patterns.why: hday_gate is one interception point with a free-regex honesty guard. This gives us a full event taxonomy with a matcher/handler split - so we can add a FileChanged or PreCompact hook without touching the gate - and the matcher rules are a real trap worth copying exactly (regex-anywhere semantics, .* required for MCP server prefixes).
patterns.build: Add hday_hooks.py with HOOK_EVENTS enum covering the subset we can actually emit: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, ConfigChange, InstructionsLoaded, FileChanged, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch. Config shape mirrors the reference: {event: [{matcher: str, if: str|None, hooks: [{type: 'command'|'http'|'python'|'prompt'|'subagent', ...}]}]}. Implement match_event(event, value) with the documented rule: if the matcher contains only [A-Za-z0-9_|] treat it as exact/|-alternatives, otherwise compile as a regex and use search() semantics. Deliver JSON input on stdin for command hooks and as a POST body for http hooks; parse stdout as text or JSON and honour permissionDecision and additionalContext. Implement exit-code mapping and an `async: true` flag that does not block the turn.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) matcher table test: 'Bash' matches only Bash; 'Edit.*' matches Edit and NotebookEdit; '^Edit$' does not match NotebookEdit; 'mcp__memory' matches nothing while 'mcp__memory__.*' matches mcp__memory__read; a matcher on an event without matcher support is ignored and the hook still fires; (b) assert a JSON stdout of {permissionDecision: 'deny'} blocks the tool and that plain-text stdout does not; (c) assert additionalContext text appears in the next model request; (d) assert an async hook returns immediately while its side effect lands later; (e) assert a hook raising an exception does not abort the turn unless its event is declared blocking.

patterns.name: Permission modes as a session baseline, layered with allow/ask/deny rules and a protected-path floor
patterns.what: A session runs in exactly one permission mode - Manual (prompt), acceptEdits, plan (read-only planning), auto (classifier-reviewed), bypassPermissions - selected by --permission-mode, by permissions.defaultMode in user or managed settings, or from the in-session mode indicator, and there is a documented precedence for which pick outranks which. Layered on top of the mode is a rule system (allow / ask / deny) where deny rules apply in every mode, and rules match commands as written rather than as resolved - a documented limitation of bash rule matching. An administrator can forbid a mode outright (disableAutoMode: 'disable' removes auto from the mode cycle and a session started with --permission-mode auto starts in Manual instead; a running session leaves auto when the setting reaches it and displays 'auto mode disabled by settings'). Working directories define the default trust boundary: reads outside them are normally prompt-free in auto mode, but the first such read prompts once and the answer can be recorded (keep allowing / block from now on, which sets permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories=true in user settings and makes file tools refuse such reads in every later session and every mode / ask again next time). Auto mode adds a classifier layer whose verdicts are explicitly enumerated: blocked-by-default (curl|bash, sending sensitive data to external endpoints, production deploys and migrations, mass deletion on cloud storage, granting IAM or repo permissions, force push, git reset --hard / checkout -- . / restore . / clean -fd / stash drop / stash clear, terraform/pulumi/cdk/terragrunt destroy, writing to a secret manager, changing DNS or TLS, merging a PR no human approved, disarming a safety guard flag, launching an agent loop without approval or sandbox, commenting out or force-passing a test or assertion that guards security behavior) and allowed-by-default (local file operations in the working directory, installing dependencies declared in lock files, reading .env and sending credentials to their matching API, read-only HTTP requests, pushes to any branch of the working repo). Critically, boundaries stated in conversation are treated as a block signal and are re-read from the transcript on each check, so a boundary can be LOST to context compaction; approvals stated in conversation only clear a block when the message names the action AND the specific thing that makes it dangerous (naming the verb alone clears nothing).
patterns.why: hday_gate has one escalation path and no notion of a session baseline, rule layers, or a floor that survives mode changes. The rule precedence (deny always wins), the compaction hazard for conversational boundaries, and the specific-thing-required approval rule are all directly implementable and directly relevant to our honesty guard.
patterns.build: Add to hday_gate: PermissionMode enum {manual, accept_edits, plan, auto, bypass} resolved by precedence (CLI flag > session override > profile setting > default) with a managed-settings disable flag per mode. Add a RuleLayer(allow=[], ask=[], deny=[]) where deny is evaluated first and applies in every mode, and rules match the command as written. Add working_directories plus block_reads_outside_working_directories as a persisted floor that file tools honour in every mode. Port the auto-mode classifier as a typed list: BLOCKED_BY_DEFAULT and ALLOWED_BY_DEFAULT pattern groups in hday_gate.policy, evaluated as data (so tests can assert membership) rather than as prose. Implement conversational boundaries as first-class session state (not transcript-scraped): Boundary(text, scope, active, lifted_by) stored on the session AND mirrored into the ledger, because our compaction is real and the reference documents that transcript-scraped boundaries get lost. Require approvals to carry a specificity record {action, dangerous_aspect} and reject approvals that name only the verb.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a deny rule blocks in every one of the five modes; (b) assert disable_auto_mode removes auto from resolution and downgrades an explicit auto request to manual; (c) assert block_reads_outside_working_directories persists after a simulated process restart and refuses reads in a different mode; (d) assert a boundary recorded then a compaction pass does not clear it (contrast: assert the transcript-scrape implementation would have lost it); (e) assert approve(action='force-push') without dangerous_aspect does not clear the block, and approve(action='force-push', dangerous_aspect='branch main') does; (f) assert each BLOCKED_BY_DEFAULT pattern is exercised by at least one fixture command.

patterns.name: Skills as frontmatter-declared capability bundles with progressive disclosure and invocation control
patterns.what: A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md whose frontmatter declares the contract: name, description, and controls including allowed-tools (pre-approve the tools the skill may use), disable-model-invocation (the model cannot auto-invoke it), user-invocable, context (including running the skill inside a forked context), agent, model, and hooks. Skills are discovered from user, project and plugin scopes. Invocation has two independent axes - the model may invoke a skill when the description matches, and the user may invoke it directly - and each axis is switchable, which is what lets you ship a skill that only humans can trigger. Skills can be executed in a subagent context, and a skill's frontmatter can carry hooks, so a skill is a portable unit of instructions + tool permissions + lifecycle behavior.
patterns.why: hermes-day skills exist but carry only prose. Adding a frontmatter contract with allowed-tools and invocation switches turns a skill into an enforceable capability bundle the manifest lane can lint - and pre-approved tools remove gate friction for the safe subset without weakening deny rules.
patterns.build: Extend the existing skill loader to parse SKILL.md frontmatter into SkillSpec(name, description, allowed_tools: list[str], disable_model_invocation: bool, user_invocable: bool, context: 'inline'|'fork', agent: str|None, model: str|None, hooks: dict). Register allowed_tools as a pre-approval set in hday_gate that is consulted AFTER deny rules (deny still wins) and only for the duration of the skill's execution. Gate model-side invocation on disable_model_invocation and expose user invocation separately in the cockpit command palette. context='fork' runs the skill body in a fresh subagent with the skill's allowed_tools rather than inheriting the parent's.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a skill with allowed_tools=['read'] gets no approval prompt for read but still hits a deny rule on write; (b) assert disable_model_invocation=True means the model's tool list omits the skill while a direct invocation still succeeds; (c) assert context='fork' starts a subagent whose tool list is the skill's allowed_tools intersected with the registry; (d) assert a skill-declared hook fires only while that skill is executing.

patterns.name: MCP client hardening: dynamic tool updates, reconnection, push messages over channels, and backgrounding
patterns.what: The MCP integration layer documents four behaviors that matter more than the happy-path connect. (1) Dynamic tool updates: when a server changes its tool set, the client picks up the change instead of requiring a reconnect, and the tool list is re-resolved. (2) Automatic reconnection with backoff: a dropped server connection is retried and the session is restored rather than surfacing as a hard failure to the model. (3) Push messages: a server can push messages into the conversation through a channel, which is how an MCP server drives the agent rather than only answering it. (4) Automatic backgrounding: a long-running tool call is moved to the background and the agent continues, with the result delivered when it lands. Tool naming is mcp__<server>__<tool>, and plugin-bundled servers get a scoped segment mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool> so matchers written against the bare server key never fire for them.
patterns.why: Our cross-native goal includes MCP, and the failure modes here are the ones that actually break harnesses: a server that adds a tool mid-session, a server that drops, and a tool that takes minutes. Backgrounding plus push channels is also the mechanism that lets a desktop cockpit stream remote results into a live turn.
patterns.build: Build hday_mcp.Client with: (a) a tool-list revision counter - on a list_changed notification, re-resolve tools and diff (added/removed) into the ledger and the model's tool list; (b) a reconnect supervisor with exponential backoff and a max-attempts budget, re-establishing the session before re-resolving tools, and recording each attempt as a ledger entry; (c) a channel abstraction where a server-pushed message is injected as a user-role message with source=mcp:<server> at a defined point in the turn; (d) automatic backgrounding: a tool call exceeding background_after_ms returns a handle to the model and delivers the result as a follow-up message, with the pending handle visible in the cockpit. Name tools mcp__<server>__<tool> and mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>, and make the hook matcher require .* for server-wide matches.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a simulated list_changed adds one tool and removes one, and the model's tool list matches the diff with two ledger entries; (b) assert a dropped connection retries with monotonically increasing backoff up to the budget and then raises a typed error; (c) assert a pushed message appears at the declared injection point and carries source=mcp:<server>; (d) assert a tool sleeping past background_after_ms returns a handle, the turn continues, and the result arrives as a follow-up; (e) assert mcp__plugin_my-plugin_db__query matches only the scoped matcher.

patterns.name: Event-driven core: topics as (type, source) pairs with typed subscriptions instead of direct agent references
patterns.what: Agent-to-agent messaging is decoupled through topics. A topic is identified by a TopicId of (type, source) where source defaults to DefaultTopicId (type='default', source='default'), so broadcasting is publishing to the default topic and direct addressing is publishing to a topic whose source is the target agent's id. Subscriptions are typed: TypeSubscription(topic_type=..., agent_type=...) means every agent of that type receives every message published to that topic type. Because the source is part of the identity, the same message type can be routed to a specific instance without the publisher knowing the instance's object - and an agent id is auto-generated from the topic source when the runtime creates the agent, which is what makes 'publish to topic (T, agent_id)' work as direct messaging. Publish is via the runtime's publish_message with the sender's id, and handlers are declared with @message_handler on a RoutedAgent.
patterns.why: hermes-day lanes call each other directly, so adding a lane means touching its callers and there is no way to observe traffic. Topics give us broadcast and direct addressing with one mechanism, and the (type, source) identity is a clean key for the decision ledger.
patterns.build: Add hday_bus.py: TopicId(type: str, source: str = 'default'), Subscription(protocol) with TypeSubscription(topic_type, agent_type) and a DefaultSubscription for the default topic. Lane agents extend a RoutedLane base with @handler(message_type) methods and an auto-generated lane_id derived from the topic source when registered. Implement publish(topic_id, message, sender_id) and broadcast(message, sender_id) on a Bus that resolves subscriptions to lane instances and records one ledger entry per delivery {topic_type, topic_source, message_type, sender, receiver, ts}. No lane may hold a direct reference to another lane - enforce it with an import/dependency test.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) two lanes subscribing to the same topic_type both receive a broadcast, in registration order; (b) a direct publish to (type, lane_id) reaches only that lane even when three lanes subscribe to the type; (c) assert lane_id is derived from the topic source on register; (d) static test: no module under lanes/ imports another lane module; (e) assert one ledger entry per delivery and zero entries for a publish with no subscribers.

patterns.name: Group chat as a manager-mediated RequestToSpeak protocol with model-based speaker selection
patterns.what: The group-chat pattern is implemented as a manager agent that owns the roster and the transcript. Participants are registered with the manager (RegisterAgent carrying the agent's topic type), and the manager runs a loop: publish a RequestToSpeak message to the selected participant, receive a GroupChatRequestPublish, publish the participant's message to the group topic, record it in the conversation, then select the next speaker and repeat until a termination condition holds. Speaker selection is pluggable - the reference implementation uses a model call over the transcript plus the roster - and SelectorGroupChat documents the high-level version of the same loop: it selects the next speaker from conversation context plus each participant's name and description, will not select the same speaker consecutively unless allow_repeated_speaker=True, supports a custom selection_function and a candidate_function that narrows the roster before selection, and supports a custom selector_prompt. Messages are broadcast to all participants, and after a task completes the conversation context is retained by the team and participants so the next task continues from it; BaseGroupChat.reset() clears it.
patterns.why: We have multi-lane turns but no shared transcript with an explicit speaker-selection step. The RequestToSpeak protocol is the piece worth copying: selection becomes a recorded, assertable event rather than an emergent property, and the consecutive-speaker guard prevents the classic 'one lane monopolizes the turn' failure.
patterns.build: Add hday_groupchat.py: GroupChatManager holding roster (lane_id -> description) and a shared transcript. Protocol messages RegisterAgent(lane_id, topic_type), RequestToSpeak(manager_id, request_id), GroupChatRequestPublish, GroupChatMessage(sender, content). select_speaker(transcript, roster, allow_repeated_speaker=False, candidate_function=None, selector_prompt=None) returns a lane_id; default implementation uses the hday judgment lane, with candidate_function narrowing the roster first. Enforce: no consecutive selection unless allow_repeated_speaker; unknown lane_id raises; every selection writes a ledger entry {kind: speaker_selected, request_id, lane_id, reason}. Expose reset() and keep the transcript across tasks by default.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert the manager never selects the same lane twice in a row while another candidate exists, and does when it is the only candidate; (b) assert candidate_function is applied before selection and a lane excluded by it can never be selected; (c) assert a scripted selector_function drives a fixed 5-message transcript deterministically (golden-file compare); (d) assert reset() empties the transcript while ledger history survives; (e) assert each RequestToSpeak produces exactly one publish from the requested lane and that an out-of-turn publish is rejected.

patterns.name: Workbench: a stateful tool collection behind one list_tools/call_tool interface, with MCP as one implementation
patterns.what: A Workbench is an interface to a COLLECTION of tools that share state and resources, distinct from a Tool which wraps one callable. The interface is two methods: list_tools() returns the current tool schemas, and call_tool(name, arguments, cancellation_token) returns a ToolResult (with to_text(), is_error, name). Because the workbench owns the state, tools can share a connection, a sandbox, or a resource pool without the agent knowing. The agent's tool loop is written out explicitly in the reference: create() with tools=await workbench.list_tools(), and while the model returns FunctionCall content, add the AssistantMessage, call the workbench per call, add a FunctionExecutionResultMessage whose entries carry call_id, content=result.to_text(), is_error=result.is_error and name, then re-create. An MCPWorkbench is a provided implementation where an MCP server is the tool collection, so local tools and remote MCP tools are reached through the same two-method interface. Cancellation is threaded through every call via the message context's cancellation token.
patterns.why: Our tools are registered flat and each owns its own setup, so shared resources (a browser, a DB handle, a sandbox) get duplicated. A workbench gives us one stateful owner per collection and makes MCP just another implementation - which is exactly the cross-native shape we want.
patterns.build: Add hday_tools.Workbench protocol {list_tools() -> list[ToolSpec], call_tool(name, arguments, cancellation) -> ToolResult} with implementations LocalWorkbench(tools, shared_state), McpWorkbench(client), and NamespacedWorkbench(name, description, members) for deferred loading. ToolResult(name, content, is_error) with to_text(). Rewrite the lane tool loop to the explicit form: create(tools=await workbench.list_tools()) -> while FunctionCall: append assistant message, call each tool, append one result message carrying call_id/is_error/name -> re-create. Thread a CancellationToken through every call and abort the loop on cancel without corrupting the message list.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a Workbench that mutates shared_state is observable from a second tool in the same collection but not from another workbench; (b) assert the result message preserves call_id, name and is_error per call (golden compare against a scripted 2-call response); (c) assert an McpWorkbench and a LocalWorkbench are interchangeable behind a fake-model fixture; (d) assert cancelling mid-loop stops before the next create() and leaves the message list well-formed; (e) assert list_tools() is re-read after a tool-set change without recreating the workbench.

patterns.name: Middleware as typed async hooks that wrap call_next, with per-turn instance state and an introspectable describe()
patterns.what: AG2 middleware defines four typed async hooks - on_turn, on_llm_call, on_tool_execution, on_human_input - each receiving the event plus a call_next continuation. A hook may call call_next(...) to continue the chain (possibly with modified arguments), return its own result to replace the call, or raise to stop. Middleware instances hold state that lives for the duration of a turn, so a middleware can accumulate across the hooks it sees within one turn and be re-created for the next. Middleware declares its configuration through describe(), which exposes the settings in a form that can be logged or asserted on - so a middleware's configuration is testable without invoking it, and configuration that must NOT leak (such as per-user approval state) is deliberately kept in context.variables rather than on the instance.
patterns.why: This is the same seam as our honesty guard but generalized: four named interception points, a continuation function instead of a boolean, and per-turn state. describe() is the piece we lack - it makes a lane's middleware configuration assertable in the manifest tests.
patterns.build: Add hday_middleware.py with abstract Middleware exposing async on_turn(event, call_next), on_llm_call(event, call_next), on_tool_execution(event, call_next), on_human_input(event, call_next), plus a state dict created fresh per turn and a describe() returning a frozen config dict. Register middleware per tool (@tool(middleware=[...])), per agent (Agent(middleware=[...])), and per run (middleware=[...] on the call), applied outermost-first in registration order. Anything that must not be introspected (approval memory) goes into the turn context's variables, never onto the instance. Port the honesty guard from a boolean check into an on_tool_execution middleware that can short-circuit by returning a result.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert the four hooks fire in the documented order for a scripted turn and that call_next receives modified arguments when a hook rewrites them; (b) assert a hook returning without calling call_next prevents the inner call (spy counter == 0); (c) assert state accumulated in on_turn is visible in on_tool_execution within the same turn and absent in the next turn; (d) assert describe() on approval_required-style middleware contains only config keys and no approval state; (e) assert nested middleware order is outermost-first.

patterns.name: Hub-and-spoke network: envelopes with Resume/Rule, WAL, append-only audit log with an open kind set, pre-decision arbiter and post-hoc listeners
patterns.what: The network model puts a hub between agents: agents do not address each other, they register with the hub and traffic moves as envelopes. Identity is a Passport plus a Resume (capabilities claimed and observed), which is what lets the hub route by capability rather than by name. Channels are created from adapter manifests with declared participants and expectations, and channel traffic is a write-ahead log. Two asymmetric seams surround every decision: a HubArbiter is consulted BEFORE the hub commits a register / channel-open / send / dispatch decision (so a policy can veto a state transition), while HubListeners are read-only observers that the hub fans state transitions out to AFTER the fact. The audit log is itself a HubListener registered first, so every state transition lands as one structured record before any other listener sees it; records are plain dicts with at least kind and at, the kind set is explicitly open for tenants to extend, it supports live tail via subscribe(cb)/unsubscribe(cb), and it can be replaced with a tenant subclass (replace_audit_log) which is registered as the first listener so audit writes still complete before other listeners observe the event. Observability is layered: pure evaluators over channel state return zero or more Violation records, and a violation handler decides what happens (audit / warn / auto_close).
patterns.why: Our decision ledger is a log, but we have no pre-commit veto point separate from post-hoc observers, and no notion of capabilities. The arbiter/listener asymmetry plus 'audit listener registered first' is a precise, copyable ordering guarantee - and the open kind set is how we can let plugins add record types without forking the ledger.
patterns.build: Add hday_hub.py: Envelope(sender, recipient, channel_id, kind, payload, id, ts); Passport(agent_id, name) and Resume(claimed_capabilities, observed_capabilities); Channel(manifest, participants, wal: list[Envelope]). Implement HubArbiter.approve(decision) -> Decision|Veto consulted before register/channel_open/send/dispatch, and HubListener.on_event(record) fanned out after commit. Make AuditLog a HubListener that the hub registers FIRST, appending one dict per transition to ledger/audit.jsonl with at least {kind, at}; expose read_all(), append(record), subscribe(cb)/unsubscribe(cb) with subscriber exceptions logged and swallowed, and replace_audit_log(custom) that re-registers the replacement at position 0. Export AUDIT_KIND_* constants and allow plugins to append new kinds. Add Expectation(name, on_violation in {'audit','warn','auto_close'}, params) evaluated by pure functions over channel state on a sweeper tick.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a vetoing arbiter prevents the state change and writes no transition record; (b) assert ordering: with a replacement audit log plus a second listener, the audit record is written before the second listener observes the event (assert call order in a spy list); (c) assert a subscriber that raises does not stop other subscribers; (d) assert a custom kind appended by a plugin is preserved by read_all(); (e) assert expectation_sweep_interval=0 disables the background loop and a manual tick fires the expected Violation and handler action.

patterns.name: Approval-gated tools that fail closed when no human channel exists
patterns.what: approval_required() is a built-in tool middleware that gates execution on human approval: when the model calls a decorated tool, the user is prompted to approve or deny before it runs, and a denial returns a message the agent can adapt to rather than an error. It takes message, denied_message, timeout, and allow_always, and returns an ApprovalRequired instance that reports its settings via describe().config (message, denied_message, timeout, allow_always) - while approval memory (which tools the user answered 'always' for) lives in context.variables and therefore never appears in the description. The fail-closed rule is the important one: approval_required() relies on the agent's hitl_hook to collect input, and with no hitl_hook configured there is nobody to ask, so context.input() raises HumanInputNotProvidedError and THE TURN ENDS - the gated tool does not run and, critically, the model is not handed a tool failure it could route around. The same applies on timeout: the turn ends with HumanInputTimeoutError, and a late answer arriving after the deadline does not release the approval. The docs also record a fixed bug pattern: timeout used to default to 30 and never fired because the hook ran inline so the clock only started after it returned; it now binds and defaults to None (wait indefinitely) so enabling a timeout does not silently start failing turns.
patterns.why: This is the most directly relevant mechanism in the whole harvest for hday_gate. Our gate currently blocks or escalates; the 'no approver -> end the turn, do not hand the model a routable failure' rule is exactly the anti-laundering property we want, and the timeout-binds-only-because-the-channel-is-async lesson is a trap we would otherwise re-introduce.
patterns.build: Port into hday_gate as middleware approval_required(message=None, denied_message=None, timeout=None, allow_always=False) returning an ApprovalRequired instance with describe().config. Gate on the turn context's hitl channel: if no hitl hook is registered, raise HumanInputNotProvidedError and END THE TURN (no tool result, no assistant continuation) rather than returning an error the model can route around. On timeout, end the turn with HumanInputTimeoutError and record the late answer as ignored. Keep approval memory in turn/session variables keyed by tool name, never on the middleware instance, and assert that describe() never contains it. Set timeout default None and document that a timeout only works because the approval channel is genuinely async.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) with no hitl hook, assert the turn ends with HumanInputNotProvidedError and the model receives NO message (assert the message list is unchanged); (b) with timeout=1 and no answer, assert HumanInputTimeoutError and that a late 'y' does not run the tool; (c) assert allow_always records 'always' in variables and a second call needs no prompt, while describe().config still reports allow_always=False as configured; (d) assert a denial returns denied_message to the model and the tool did not run; (e) regression: assert the timeout clock starts when the prompt is emitted, not when the hook returns (fixture where the hook sleeps past the timeout).

patterns.name: Task guardrails as a (passed, value) contract with feedback-as-retry and bounded retries
patterns.what: A Task can carry guardrail (single) or guardrails (a list, executed sequentially). Each guardrail is either a callable or a natural-language string; a string is turned into an LLM guardrail automatically. The callable contract is a tuple: (bool, Any) - True with the (possibly transformed) output means proceed, and False with a value means the value is treated as feedback and the task is retried with that feedback, which is why the same hook both validates and repairs output. guardrail_max_retries bounds the loop. Because guardrails are a list, validation and transformation compose: an early guardrail can normalize the output that later guardrails then check.
patterns.why: hday_gate returns a verdict but has no repair loop, so a bad lane output either passes or fails the turn. The (passed, value) contract plus feedback-as-retry is a small change that turns validation into a bounded self-correction, and string guardrails let us declare a check in a manifest without writing code.
patterns.build: Add hday_gate.TaskGuardrail = Callable[[TaskOutput], tuple[bool, Any]]. Task(guardrails=[...], guardrail_max_retries=N). Runner: run guardrails sequentially over the candidate output; each guardrail returning (True, v) replaces the working output with v; (False, feedback) aborts the chain and re-runs the task with `feedback` appended to the prompt; after guardrail_max_retries exhausted, fail the turn with a typed GuardrailExhausted carrying the last feedback and the full guardrail history. Accept a plain string guardrail by compiling it into an LLM guardrail that asks the judgment lane for a (bool, reason) verdict. Record every attempt in the ledger {attempt, guardrail, passed, feedback}.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a guardrail returning (True, transformed) mutates the output seen by the next guardrail in the list; (b) assert (False, 'needs a citation') re-runs the task with that exact feedback in the prompt and succeeds on attempt 2; (c) assert guardrail_max_retries=2 stops after exactly 3 attempts and raises GuardrailExhausted; (d) assert a string guardrail is compiled and its verdict is routed through the fake judgment lane; (e) assert the ledger holds one record per attempt in order.

patterns.name: Hook system with typed interception points, four interception verbs, and fail-open for unrelated exceptions
patterns.what: Execution hooks are typed by InterceptionPoint and registered per agent, per tool, or crew-wide, with agents=/tools= scoping filters. A hook may intercept in four ways: proceed (let the call continue, optionally with modified arguments), mutate, replace (substitute the result), or abort. Aborting raises HookAborted carrying a reason and a source, which is a typed signal rather than a generic exception. Crucially, the failure policy is asymmetric: HookAborted is the deliberate control-flow path, while any OTHER exception raised inside a hook is fail-open - the hook is treated as a non-event and execution continues, so a broken observability hook cannot take down a run. Hooks also emit a HookDispatchedEvent for telemetry, which makes hook activity observable without instrumenting each hook.
patterns.why: Our gate is a single choke point and any exception in it is a hard failure. Splitting 'deliberate veto' (typed, aborts) from 'hook bug' (logged, continues) is exactly the robustness posture we want, and HookDispatchedEvent gives us hook-level telemetry for free.
patterns.build: Add hday_hooks.InterceptionPoint enum (agent_start, agent_end, llm_before, llm_after, tool_before, tool_after, task_start, task_end, turn_end) and register(point, fn, agents=None, tools=None, crew_wide=False). Implement the four verbs: Hooks.proceed(args=None), Hooks.mutate(args), Hooks.replace(result), Hooks.abort(reason, source) raising HookAborted. The dispatcher catches HookAborted and honours it; it catches every other exception, logs it without payload, and CONTINUES the call (fail-open). Emit a HookDispatchedEvent(point, hook_name, outcome, duration_ms) into the ledger for every dispatch, including fail-open ones.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert Hooks.abort raises HookAborted and the call does not proceed; (b) assert a hook raising ValueError is logged, the call proceeds, and a HookDispatchedEvent with outcome='error' is recorded; (c) assert mutate changes the arguments the executor receives; (d) assert replace short-circuits the executor (spy counter == 0) and its value is returned; (e) assert agents=['lane-a'] scoping means the hook never fires for lane-b; (f) assert exactly one HookDispatchedEvent per dispatch.

patterns.name: LLM-collapsed human feedback that routes a flow through declared outcomes
patterns.what: A @human_feedback(...) decorator on a flow method declares the outcomes the human can produce: emit=[...] names the branches, llm= names the model that interprets the free-form human reply, and default_outcome= names the fallback when the reply matches nothing. The human types prose; the model collapses it into exactly one of the declared outcomes; the outcome is what @listen/@router conditions branch on. The result is surfaced as a HumanFeedbackResult dataclass carrying both the raw text and the resolved outcome, and there is an async provider form so a webhook or UI can supply the answer without blocking the flow thread. This keeps the flow graph finite (only N branches exist) while letting the human speak naturally.
patterns.why: Our cockpit feedback is free text that a human reads, and gate escalations currently return raw prose. Declaring N outcomes and letting the judgment lane collapse prose into one of them makes human feedback machine-routable without a rigid form.
patterns.build: Add hday_gate.human_feedback(emit=[...], llm=None, default_outcome=None) decorating a step. On invocation, emit a feedback request to the cockpit, receive free text (sync provider or async provider for webhook/UI), call the judgment lane with a schema constraining the answer to the declared outcomes, and return HumanFeedbackResult(raw_text, outcome, matched: bool). Steps then declare routing as on(outcome) handlers, so the graph has exactly len(emit) branches. If the model returns nothing matching, use default_outcome and record matched=False in the ledger.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert free text 'yeah go ahead but tighten the intro' collapses to the declared 'approve' outcome via a fake judgment lane; (b) assert text matching nothing yields default_outcome with matched=False; (c) assert the returned object carries both raw_text and outcome; (d) assert only the declared outcomes can route (an undeclared outcome raises); (e) assert the async provider path resolves a webhook-supplied answer without blocking.

patterns.name: Crews versus flows: autonomous collaboration as one node inside a deterministic orchestration graph
patterns.what: The architecture draws a hard line between two execution models and then composes them. A Crew is an autonomous, role-based unit: agents with roles and goals collaborate under a process (sequential, or hierarchical where a manager LLM or manager agent plans and delegates), and the crew decides its own internal path. A Flow is an event-driven graph: methods are marked @start, @listen(...) and @router, conditions compose with or_()/and_(), and the flow owns explicit state that is passed between steps. The composition rule is that a crew can be kicked off as a step inside a flow, and a flow can be invoked from within a crew - so autonomy is a bounded node inside a deterministic graph rather than the top-level control structure. Flows additionally support persistence: a persisted flow started with a stable id resumes prior state, while a distinct restore-from id forks a new run from a previous state, and a flow can be run synchronously or streamed.
patterns.why: hermes-day is closer to a flow already, but our lane autonomy has no boundary. Making 'autonomous lane group' an explicit node type inside a deterministic graph - rather than the whole architecture - is the structural lesson, and it maps directly onto the router lane.
patterns.build: Add hday_flow.py: Flow with @start, @listen(*events), @router decorators, or_()/and_() condition combinators, and a typed FlowState object threaded through steps. Add a CrewStep node type that wraps a group of lanes with a declared process ('sequential' | 'hierarchical' with manager_lane) and returns a single result to the flow. Enforce the boundary in the manifest: a CrewStep may not declare flow-level routing, and a Flow may not be started from inside a CrewStep except as a declared sub-flow. Support flow persistence with kickoff(state_id=...) to resume and restore_from_state_id=... to fork.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert or_(a, b) fires on either event and and_(a, b) only after both, in either order; (b) assert a CrewStep returns exactly one result object to the flow regardless of how many lanes ran inside it; (c) assert manifest validation rejects a CrewStep declaring flow-level routing; (d) assert kickoff with an existing state_id resumes rather than restarting (assert step-execution counts); (e) assert restore_from_state_id produces a new state_id with fork lineage.

patterns.name: Hierarchical memory: LLM-inferred scopes, composite scoring with tunable decay, and private per-agent views
patterns.what: Memory is one system with hierarchical scopes rather than several stores: the built-in scopes are short-term, long-term, entity and external, and writes are routed into the right scope by an LLM that infers where a fact belongs. Retrieval is scored by a composite rather than raw similarity - semantic similarity combined with recency and importance weights, with a tunable recency half-life in days - so a recent but only loosely similar item can outrank an older near-exact match. The API is uniform across scopes (remember, recall, forget, extract_memories, tree) and a scope(path) accessor exposes a private view so one agent can be given its own memory namespace without a second store. Extraction happens automatically after a task and recall is injected automatically before one, so the agent does not have to manage memory explicitly.
patterns.why: Our ctxscore is a single similarity-ish score. Adding importance and recency with an explicit half-life parameter, plus LLM-inferred scope routing, gives us memory that degrades gracefully instead of returning stale exact matches - and scope() gives lanes private memory without new storage.
patterns.build: Extend hday_ctxscore into hday_memory.py with scopes short_term, long_term, entity, external and a router that uses the judgment lane to classify a candidate fact into a scope (with a deterministic fallback rule). Scoring: score = w_semantic * cosine + w_recency * 0.5**(age_days / recency_half_life_days) + w_importance * importance, all weights and the half-life configurable in the lane manifest. Implement remember/recall/forget/extract_memories/tree, auto-extract after each task and auto-inject a recall block before each task, and a scope(path) accessor returning a private view bound to one lane.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert the composite score ordering flips when recency_half_life_days is lowered (fixture with one fresh low-similarity and one old high-similarity item); (b) assert scope('lane-a') cannot read an item written to scope('lane-b') (expect empty result); (c) assert the deterministic fallback router classifies a fixture fact into the expected scope when the judgment lane is stubbed to fail; (d) assert extract_memories runs after a task and the injected recall block appears before the next task's prompt; (e) assert tree() returns the scope hierarchy with counts matching writes.

patterns.name: Team modes: the orchestration pattern is a swap-in enum, and members are resolved by stable id at run time
patterns.what: A team's delegation behavior is selected by a mode enum rather than by rewriting members: TeamMode.coordinate (default) has the leader select members, formulate each member's task, and synthesize results; TeamMode.route has the leader pick one member and return that member's response directly (no synthesis step, lower latency); TeamMode.broadcast sends the same task to every member; TeamMode.tasks has the leader build and execute a shared task list until the goal is complete. Two orthogonal flags survive as legacy: determine_input_for_members=False passes the raw user content to members instead of letting the leader formulate a task (and it applies across coordinate, route and broadcast), and respond_directly=True returns member responses without leader synthesis. Member identity is explicit - members should carry stable id values because member selection and run tracking are keyed on them - and members can also come from callable factories resolved at run time, so the roster is not fixed at construction. The leader can still answer directly or use its own tools in any mode.
patterns.why: Our router is one fixed strategy. Making the orchestration pattern a declared enum (coordinate/route/broadcast/tasks) means we can A/B strategies per lane without touching member code, and 'stable member ids because tracking is keyed on them' is a correctness detail our ledger needs.
patterns.build: Add hday_router.TeamMode {coordinate, route, broadcast, tasks} and lane_group(name, members=[...], mode=TeamMode.coordinate, determine_input_for_members=True, respond_directly=False). Require every member to declare a stable id and fail manifest validation if missing or duplicated. Implement members= as a list or as a callable factory resolved at run time. Record the mode and the resolved member ids on every delegation ledger entry so a strategy change is visible in the audit trail.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert route mode returns the member's response unchanged with no synthesis call (assert the leader's synthesis prompt was never built); (b) assert broadcast sends the identical task object to every member and coordinate sends per-member tasks; (c) assert determine_input_for_members=False passes raw user content for coordinate, route and broadcast; (d) assert tasks mode executes a shared list to completion and its final task list is recorded; (e) assert a member without a stable id fails validation and a duplicate id fails validation; (f) assert a callable factory is invoked once per run, not at construction.

patterns.name: Session storage keyed by session_id with a session_type discriminator, separate run tables, and storage control
patterns.what: Persistence is opt-in by attaching a database, and everything then hangs off a session_id. A hydrated session carries session_id, the owner id (agent_id / team_id / workflow_id depending on owner type), user_id, per-owner data blobs (session_data, agent_data, team_data, workflow_data), metadata, runs, summary, created_at and updated_at. The physical layout separates concerns: session metadata lives in a session table (default agno_sessions) while run records live in a separate runs table (default agno_runs) and are loaded into session.runs on hydration - runs is not a column on the session table - and a session_type discriminator column distinguishes agent, team and workflow sessions, so one storage layer serves all three owner types. Tables are created on first relevant operation if absent, session_table and runs_table are independently configurable (documented for environment isolation), and the same get_session(session_id=...) interface exists on Agent, Team and Workflow. There is also documented storage control for choosing what gets persisted, and session summaries for condensing long conversations.
patterns.why: Our ledger mixes conversation content and run metadata in one append-only file. Splitting session metadata from run records, keying on a session_id with an owner-type discriminator, and making 'what gets persisted' a setting gives us retention control the cockpit needs.
patterns.build: Add hday_store.py: Session(session_id, owner_id, owner_type, user_id, session_data, owner_data, metadata, runs, summary, created_at, updated_at) with owner_type in {agent, team, workflow} as a discriminator column. Two tables, hday_sessions and hday_runs, with independently configurable names, created on first use if absent; hydration loads runs into session.runs. Expose get_session(session_id) identically from agent, lane_group and flow objects. Add a storage_control config listing which message classes are persisted (e.g. skip reasoning traces and raw tool payloads) and a session summary job that condenses long sessions.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert runs is not a column on hday_sessions and hydration reconstructs session.runs from hday_runs in order; (b) assert an agent session, a lane_group session and a flow session are distinguishable by owner_type while get_session is the same call shape; (c) assert custom session_table/runs_table names are honoured and a fresh DB creates both tables on first write; (d) assert storage_control excluding tool payloads means the persisted run has the tool call but not its payload; (e) assert a session summary is produced for a session past the configured length.

patterns.name: Human-in-the-loop as a persisted pause with a three-level requirement tree and a continue_run resumption loop
patterns.what: When a workflow pauses for HITL it exposes the pause through three nested objects and the caller reads them to find out what is being asked, resolves the innermost ones, and calls continue_run. WorkflowRunOutput carries is_paused and pause_kind ('step' | 'executor' | None) plus requirement collections that name what is pending: steps_requiring_confirmation (confirm/reject), steps_requiring_user_input (values), steps_requiring_output_review, steps_requiring_route (route selection) and steps_requiring_executor_resolution (an agent/team tool needing resolution). Below that, a StepRequirement object describes one step's requirement (requires_confirmation and friends), and below that executor-level requirements describe a tool-level gate (for example tool_execution.requires_confirmation, or confirmation/confirmed pairs to approve a @tool(requires_confirmation=True)). The documented driver is a loop: while run_output.is_paused, resolve the pending requirements, then run_output = workflow.continue_run(run_output). Because pause state is part of the run output that is persisted, a pause survives the process and can be resumed later.
patterns.why: Our gate escalations are in-memory and a restart loses them. The three-level requirement tree is a precise data model for 'what is this turn waiting for', and pause_kind step-versus-executor is exactly the distinction between our gate-level and tool-level approvals.
patterns.build: Extend the gate/runner with RunOutput.is_paused, pause_kind in {'step','executor',None}, and requirement collections steps_requiring_confirmation / _user_input / _output_review / _route / _executor_resolution. Add StepRequirement(step_id, requires_confirmation, requires_user_input, requires_route, ...) and an executor-requirement shape for tool gates (tool_execution.requires_confirmation; confirmation + confirmed to approve). Persist pause state with the run so it survives restart, and provide the documented driver loop: while run_output.is_paused: resolve pending requirements; run_output = continue_run(run_output). Surface the requirement tree in the cockpit so the UI renders what is pending rather than a generic 'blocked'.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a step-level confirmation pause sets pause_kind='step' and populates steps_requiring_confirmation only; (b) assert a @tool(requires_confirmation=True) gate sets pause_kind='executor' and populates the executor requirement; (c) assert resolving only the inner requirements and calling continue_run resumes correctly, and that calling continue_run with an unresolved requirement raises; (d) assert pause state survives a serialized restart (write, reload, continue_run, same outcome); (e) assert the loop terminates exactly when no requirements remain.

patterns.name: Tool hooks as ordered wrappers with injected run context, plus observe-only pre/post hooks
patterns.what: A tool hook receives the function name, the wrapped function call, and the arguments, and controls execution by what it does with the wrapped callable: calling function_call(**arguments) continues the chain (possibly with mutated arguments), while raising or returning another value stops or replaces the call. Hooks are assigned per agent or per team and apply to every tool call that owner makes, or per tool via the decorator, and a list is applied in order with the FIRST hook as the outermost layer. Hooks can receive a RunContext by declaring a supported parameter name, giving access to session state, dependencies and metadata - the documented pattern is to read a value out of session_state and rewrite an argument before continuing the chain. Alongside wrapping hooks there are observe-only pre_hook and post_hook callbacks that receive the FunctionCall object (function, arguments, result); exceptions in these are logged and execution CONTINUES, and the docs state explicitly that they are not equivalent to a wrapping gate - deliberate aborts need a supported run-control exception such as StopAgentRun.
patterns.why: Two things here are directly usable: ordered outermost-first wrappers with an explicit continuation callable (cleaner than a boolean), and the documented split between observe-only hooks (fail-open, for logging) and wrapping hooks (can stop). We currently conflate logging and gating in one place.
patterns.build: Add hday_tools.hook(fn) with a documented parameter-name convention: agent/lane, team, run_context for injection, name/function_name, function/func/function_call, args/arguments. Wrap order = outermost-first in registration order, and the chain continues only when the hook calls function_call(**arguments); raising aborts, returning a value replaces. Add pre_hook/post_hook decorator kwargs receiving a FunctionCall(function, arguments, result) that are observe-only: exceptions are logged and execution continues, and deliberate aborts must use StopRun from hday.exceptions. Document in the gate module that pre/post hooks must never be relied on to block.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert hooks=[outer, inner] runs outer first and that mutating arguments in outer is visible to inner and to the tool; (b) assert a hook that raises prevents the tool from running and propagates the exception; (c) assert a hook that returns a value replaces the tool result; (d) assert a pre_hook raising ValueError is logged and the tool still runs; (e) assert run_context injection exposes session_state mutations to the tool body; (f) assert StopRun from a post_hook aborts the run (the documented deliberate-abort path).

patterns.name: Workflow as a typed chain DSL where step ids are the data keys
patterns.what: A workflow is built by chaining typed steps: createStep({id, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute}) and then .then(step), .parallel([...]), .branch([...]), .map(fn), terminated by .commit(). Because steps are declared with zod input and output schemas, the graph is type-checked at composition time, and step ids are the addressing scheme for data: after .parallel() or .branch() the result is an object keyed by child step id, a following step reads the previous step's value through inputData, and a specific result is retrieved with getStepResult(step). .branch() requires every branch to share the same inputSchema and outputSchema because branching must keep schemas consistent, only the first branch whose condition is true executes, and its output is keyed by that step's id. .map() exists precisely to reshape the keyed output of parallel/branch into the input shape the next step needs, and it also applies after .then(). Failure handling is a declared property of the parallel step rather than ad-hoc try/catch.
patterns.why: Our lane sequencing is imperative code, so a partially completed turn has no declared shape. A chain DSL with schemas at every edge makes the whole turn type-checkable and makes 'what does lane N receive' a schema, not a convention - and step-id-keyed outputs give the cockpit a stable addressing scheme.
patterns.build: Add hday_flow.Step(id, input_schema, output_schema, execute) and a Workflow builder with .then(step), .parallel([steps]), .branch([steps]) (each carrying a condition), .map(fn), .dowhile(...), .foreach(...), .commit(). Validate at composition time that adjacent schemas are compatible and that all .branch() members share input and output schemas. Outputs of parallel/branch are dicts keyed by child step id, and expose get_step_result(step). Persist the executed step ids and their schema-validated outputs in the ledger so a run can be replayed step by step.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert composing .then(a).then(b) with incompatible a.output_schema/b.input_schema raises at build time, not at run time; (b) assert .branch() with mismatched member schemas is rejected; (c) assert only the first matching branch executes and the output dict is keyed by that step's id; (d) assert .parallel() output is keyed by every child id and get_step_result returns the same object; (e) assert .map() after .parallel() reshapes into the next step's input_schema and a mismatch fails validation; (f) assert a declared failure policy on .parallel() is honoured when one child raises.

patterns.name: Suspend and resume with schema-validated resume data and persisted snapshots
patterns.what: A step can pause itself: it declares a resumeSchema in addition to inputSchema/outputSchema, and inside execute it calls suspend() (returning suspend({...})) when its resume condition is unmet. Suspension saves the current execution state as a snapshot in the configured storage provider, so it persists across deployments and restarts. run.resume({step, resumeData}) restarts from that step with resumeData validated against the step's resumeSchema; the step object can be passed for full type-safety or a step id string when the id comes from user input or a database; when only one step is suspended the step argument can be omitted and the last suspended step resumes; and resuming with only a runId requires creating the run instance first via createRun({runId}). Because resume is an ordinary call, it can be invoked from an HTTP endpoint, an event handler, or a timer - which is what makes 'wait for a human, an API callback, or a delay' the same mechanism.
patterns.why: Our escalation path blocks the turn in memory. suspend()/resume() with schema-validated resume data turns 'waiting for a human' into a persisted, resumable state that survives a restart and can be driven from the cockpit over HTTP.
patterns.build: Add resume_schema to hday_flow.Step and a suspend(payload) call inside execute. On suspend, persist a Snapshot(run_id, step_id, state, created_at) through the existing storage provider and return a suspended run handle. Implement run.resume(step=None, resume_data=None, run_id=None): validate resume_data against the step's resume_schema (reject with a typed error on mismatch), locate the step by object or by id string, default to the last suspended step when omitted, and require create_run(run_id=...) when only a run id is known. Expose a POST /runs/{run_id}/resume endpoint for the cockpit and a timer-based resume for timeout policies.
