patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert suspend() writes exactly one snapshot and the run reports suspended with the step id; (b) assert resume with resume_data violating resume_schema raises a typed validation error and leaves the snapshot intact; (c) assert resume by step id string and by step object behave identically; (d) assert omitting the step resumes the last suspended step when exactly one is suspended and raises when several are; (e) assert resume from a re-loaded process (serialize, restart, resume) produces the same completion; (f) assert the HTTP endpoint path performs the same validation as the in-process call.

patterns.name: Six-seam processor pipeline with an abort tripwire that can request a retry
patterns.what: Processors attach to an agent as inputProcessors / outputProcessors and expose up to six interception methods at different granularities: processInput (once at the start of agent execution; receives messages, systemMessages and an abort() function; returns a replacement message array or {messages, systemMessages}), processInputStep (at EVERY step of the agentic loop including tool-call continuations, enabling per-step model switching or tool-choice changes), processLLMRequest (rewrite the request immediately before the provider call, with prompt, model, stepNumber, steps, state and abort()), processOutputStep (after each LLM step, to validate and optionally request a retry), processOutputStream (per streamed chunk, with per-chunk drop versus abort()), and processOutputResult (the final result). abort() is the tripwire and emits a normal tripwire response that stops the call; abort('reason', {retry: true}) requests a retry instead of a hard stop. Output methods share a state object that lives for the lifetime of one request, keyed by the processor's id so each processor sees only its own data, created fresh for every generate()/stream() call. Execution order relative to memory is documented and matters: an output guardrail that calls abort() skips memory processors so the rejected messages are not saved. prepareStep() is a shorthand that wraps processInputStep() for the common case.
patterns.why: Our ctxscore runs at one point. Six named seams - especially processInputStep for per-step policy changes and processOutputStep with retry - let us enforce budget and honesty checks per step instead of once per turn, and the shared per-request state object is the right place for accumulators.
patterns.build: Add hday_processors.py with a Processor base exposing async process_input, process_input_step, process_llm_request, process_output_step, process_output_stream, process_output_result, each receiving (payload, abort, state) and returning a replacement payload or None. abort(reason, retry=False) raises/returns a Tripwire that either stops the call or requests one more attempt. state is a dict created per request and namespaced by processor id. Wire input_processors and output_processors on the lane config, document and enforce the ordering rule that an output tripwire skips memory writes so rejected content is never persisted, and add prepare_step(fn) as the shorthand for process_input_step.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert process_input_step fires once per loop iteration including after tool calls, while process_input fires exactly once (count via spy); (b) assert state written in process_output_stream is readable in process_output_result and is empty in a second request; (c) assert state namespacing: two processors with different ids never see each other's keys; (d) assert abort(retry=True) causes exactly one retry and abort() without retry stops; (e) assert an output tripwire prevents the memory write (assert the store is unchanged); (f) assert prepare_step is equivalent to a process_input_step processor.

patterns.name: Evals as gates plus thresholds with a three-valued verdict
patterns.what: Evals add severity semantics to a scored run. runEvals({data, target, gates, scorers}) separates hard requirements from tracked metrics: gates are scorers that must average 1.0 across all data items or the run fails, and scorers are tracked metrics that may carry a threshold. A threshold is either a number (minimum) or an object with min and/or max - max exists specifically for scorers where a high score is bad (hallucination, toxicity) and {min, max} expresses a band. The verdict is computed after all items are processed: 'failed' if any gate averaged below 1.0, 'scored' if all gates passed but some threshold was missed, 'passed' if all gates scored 1.0 and all thresholds were met; the verdict field is OMITTED entirely when no gates or threshold-bearing scorers are configured, or when every configured gate and threshold returned notScorable() (no numeric evidence), in which case scores and summary are still returned. Gates run before regular scorers on each item, and a gate-only run is allowed (scorers is optional when at least one gate is present) which is documented for deterministic CI checks; a run with neither gates nor scorers throws. Results are exposed as gateResults [{id, passed, score}] and thresholdResults [{id, passed, averageScore, threshold}] so CI can print exactly which gate failed.
patterns.why: This is the missing piece for our test story: 267 tests currently assert behavior, but nothing aggregates 'must-pass' versus 'nice-to-have' into one verdict. Gates + the three-valued verdict gives CI a single honest signal, and 'notScorable omits the verdict rather than passing' is precisely the anti-laundering rule we care about.
patterns.build: Add hday_evals.run_evals(data, target, gates=[], scorers=[]) with Gate(id, fn) requiring an average of 1.0 and Scorer(id, fn, threshold: float | {'min':..,'max':..}). Compute verdict in {passed, scored, failed} after all items, OMIT the verdict when there are no gates or threshold-bearing scorers or when every one returned not_scorable(), and expose gate_results and threshold_results. Allow a gate-only run (scorers optional) and raise when neither is supplied. Wire a CI entry point that exits 1 on 'failed', warns on 'scored', and prints the failing gate ids. Mirror mastra's naming in the test helpers so existing tests can migrate incrementally.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert a gate averaging 0.99 yields verdict='failed' and a gate averaging 1.0 yields at least 'scored'; (b) assert a max-only threshold fails on a high score (toxicity fixture) and a {min,max} band fails outside the band; (c) assert the verdict key is ABSENT when all gates and thresholds return not_scorable() (assert 'verdict' not in result); (d) assert a run with neither gates nor scorers raises; (e) assert a bare scorer appears in scores but does not change the verdict; (f) assert gate_results ids match the failing gate printed by the CI entry point.

patterns.name: Delegation hooks that can rewrite, bound, or reject a subagent delegation, with a copied request context
patterns.what: Subagents are declared on the parent as an agents map, and the parent decides when to delegate using its own instructions plus each subagent's description - the supervisor pattern. Delegation is interceptable through a delegation option (set in the agent's defaultOptions or per call) with onDelegationStart(context), which is called before the parent delegates and returns an object controlling it: proceed: true to allow, proceed: false with a rejectionReason to reject (the reason is handed back to the parent, which can then synthesize instead), modifiedPrompt to rewrite what the subagent receives, and modifiedMaxSteps to bound the subagent's own iteration count. The context exposes primitiveId (which subagent), prompt, iteration (current iteration number) and requestContext - and the iteration field is what lets a hook implement 'reject delegation after N iterations and force synthesis'. Request context is shallow-copied at the delegation boundary, excluding run-scoped identity keys, so entries set or deleted during the subagent run do not affect the parent, and the hook can set entries on context.requestContext to pass values down. There is a further delegation option group beyond onDelegationStart (message filtering and completion scoring are documented alongside it).
patterns.why: This is the most directly copyable mechanism for our delegation path: a single hook that can rewrite the delegated prompt, cap the child's budget, and reject with a reason the parent can act on - plus the request-context copy rule that prevents a child from mutating parent state.
patterns.build: Add delegation={'onDelegationStart': fn} on the lane group and per call. DelegationContext(primitive_id, prompt, iteration, request_context). The hook returns {proceed: bool, rejection_reason: str|None, modified_prompt: str|None, modified_max_steps: int|None}. Implement: rejection returns the reason to the parent as a tool error it can act on rather than aborting the turn; modified_prompt replaces the child's prompt; modified_max_steps caps the child's loop; and request_context is a SHALLOW COPY at the boundary so child writes never leak to the parent (assert this with a mutation test). Record every delegation decision and its modifications in the ledger.
patterns.test: Deterministic: (a) assert proceed=False delivers rejection_reason to the parent and the child lane never runs (spy counter == 0); (b) assert modified_prompt is what the child receives (capture the child's first request); (c) assert modified_max_steps caps the child's iterations at exactly N; (d) assert iteration increments across repeated delegations in one turn and a hook rejecting at iteration > 8 forces synthesis; (e) assert a child setting a request_context key is not visible to the parent afterwards, while a key set by the hook IS visible to the child.
